There are no nonconvex Euclidean regular tessellations in any number of dimensions.

===Polytope elements===
The elements of a polytope can be considered according to either their own dimensionality or how many dimensions "down" they are from the body.

*[[Vertex (geometry)|Vertex]], a 0-dimensional element
*[[Edge (geometry)|Edge]], a 1-dimensional element
*[[Face (geometry)|Face]], a 2-dimensional element
*[[Cell (geometry)|Cell]], a 3-dimensional element
*[[Hypercell]] or Teron, a 4-dimensional element
*[[Facet (geometry)|Facet]], an (''n''-1)-dimensional element
*[[Ridge (geometry)|Ridge]], an (''n''-2)-dimensional element
*[[Peak (geometry)|Peak]], an (''n''-3)-dimensional element

For example, in a [[polyhedron]] (3-dimensional polytope), a face is a facet, an edge is a ridge, and a vertex is a peak.

*[[Vertex figure]]: not itself an element of a polytope, but a diagram showing how the elements meet.

===Tessellations===

The classical convex polytopes may be considered [[tessellation]]s, or tilings, of spherical space. Tessellations of euclidean and hyperbolic space may also be considered regular polytopes. Note that an 'n'-dimensional polytope actually tessellates a space of one dimension less. For example, the (three-dimensional) platonic solids tessellate the 'two'-dimensional 'surface' of the sphere.

===Zero dimension===
*[[Point (geometry)|Point]]

===One-dimensional regular polytope===
There is only one polytope in 1 dimension, whose boundaries are the two endpoints of a [[line segment]], represented by the empty [[Schläfli symbol]] {}.
